# What the Architect Owns {#sec-what-architect-owns}

::: {.epigraph}
> "The second irony is that the designer who tries to eliminate the operator still leaves the operator to do the tasks which the designer cannot think how to automate."
>
> — Lisanne Bainbridge, *Ironies of Automation* [@Bainbridge1983Ironies, p. 775]
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
**Governing question:** *If AI can perform substantial design work, what do architects still contribute and remain responsible for?*

**Core thesis:** *Architectural ownership resides in framing problems, setting abstractions, judging cross-layer trade-offs, and governing commitment to silicon.*
:::

Architects turn product needs into system designs. They choose the problem, develop abstractions and alternatives, connect software behavior to physical consequences, and reconcile the trade-offs across components. An AI-native design system may contribute to all of that work, including proposing better formulations and organizations. The architect's responsibility is to develop and defend a coherent system recommendation, even if automation can generate the register-transfer level (RTL), search the configurations, and complete the implementation checks.

That recommendation and the decision to act on it remain distinct (@fig-ch11-cover-map). A *technical recommendation* explains whether a candidate serves the product's requirements, what alternatives were considered, and what remains uncertain. *Commitment authority* belongs to a named person authorized to freeze an interface, accept residual risk, or tape out the design. A leading-edge mask set alone is estimated in the tens of millions of dollars [@Patel2022MaskSetCosts], so fabrication commits substantial capital before any wafer is measured. Neither a favorable tool report nor a demonstrated workflow advantage (@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect) makes that decision automatically.

![**Architectural ownership separates candidate evaluation from commitment authority.** An AI-native design system and domain specialists explore candidate spaces and verify implementations, but architects own problem formulation, abstraction boundaries, and cross-layer trade-offs. The resulting system recommendation provides qualified evidence to an authorized organizational decision maker rather than committing resources automatically.](images/ch11-cover-map.svg){#fig-ch11-cover-map width="100%" fig-alt="Chapter overview diagram in which substantial AI-native design work and architectural ownership remain distinct from a named commitment authority inside an accountable organization."}

The recommendation itself rests on checks that other people run. Domain specialists establish what their checks support, and the architect connects those findings across the system and investigates interactions that no single check covers. The recommendation remains bounded by the implementation and conditions those checks cover. Integration, deployment, and later changes to the workload or operating conditions can invalidate that basis, so architectural ownership includes deciding when to reopen the recommendation. Delegation must therefore preserve the technical understanding and access needed to revise the design and its recommendation.

## Delegating Without Losing Technical Contact {#sec-delegating-without-losing-contact}

Delegation does not remove responsibility for deciding what to build. As Fred Brooks observed, specifying what to build remains a central difficulty of engineering [@Brooks1986NoSilverBullet]. An automated system may help formulate the problem, propose alternatives, and assemble evidence for a recommendation. The people responsible for the product still decide whether that recommendation addresses the right needs and warrants commitment. This division does not depend on human proposals being better than automated ones.

In conventional workflows, engineers build the judgment to evaluate a recommendation by writing RTL, inspecting waveforms, and iterating with electronic design automation (EDA) tools. That hands-on contact shows them directly how microarchitectural choices turn into routing congestion and timing slack. When a team delegates candidate drafting, macro floorplanning, and regression sweeps to automated loops, the contact moves away from the engineer. The architect need not repeat every automated step by hand, but must still be able to inspect the specific traces, floorplans, and assumptions that could overturn the recommendation.

Four questions help determine how much work can be delegated and what must be checked before acting on its results:

1. **Observability**: Can the architect inspect the candidate, its evaluation conditions, and the traces supporting the recommendation?
2. **Reversibility**: Which changes can be rolled back cleanly, and which would require costly rework once accepted?
3. **Independent checks**: What checks could expose errors in the proposal or its evaluation, and which assumptions do those checks share with the automated loop?
4. **Bounded consequences**: Which cross-layer effects have been evaluated, and which remain outside the study's scope?

The answers depend on the scope of the delegated work (@sec-three-operational-layers). An engineer can inspect a generated arithmetic block and restore its previous revision. A broad hardware–software redesign instead requires access to interface contracts, execution traces, counterexamples, and physical reports; line-by-line inspection alone cannot establish that its components work together. In either case, the team must preserve a known integration version and control which changes may enter the product design.

Reversibility becomes especially important as decisions approach interface freeze. A bounded array-mapping sweep or a focused tool run leaves interfaces open. Freezing an instruction set architecture (ISA) contract or fixing the physical-layer lane count on a 2.5D Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) link[^fn-ucie-phy-c11] hardens assumptions across compiler runtimes, memory hierarchies, RTL, floorplans, and product thermals at once. Before the responsible lead authorizes such a freeze, the architect must reconcile evidence across every one of those coupled layers.

[^fn-ucie-phy-c11]: **Die-to-die physical layers and interconnect budgeting**: In multi-die systems, Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) defines standard physical layer (PHY) lane allocations, die-edge beachfront reach, and bump pitches (typically $100\text{--}130\ \mu\text{m}$ for standard organic package substrates and $25\text{--}55\ \mu\text{m}$ for advanced 2.5D packaging such as silicon interposers or bridges). Freezing PHY lane counts constrains die-edge allocation, substrate routing layers, and escape routing. Bandwidth can still change through supported link rates within the qualified operating envelope; adding lanes or exceeding those capabilities may require an expensive package redesign. [@UCIeConsortium2024Overview]

Reconciling those layers requires direct technical contact across tool boundaries. Without that contact, an engineer has no basis for calibrating trust in automation, and human-factors research names the two resulting failures *misuse* (inappropriate reliance on automation) and *disuse* (neglecting automation capabilities entirely) [@ParasuramanRiley1997HumansAutomation]. Good abstractions do not remove the need. Logic synthesis and hardware construction languages provide powerful ways to express and implement designs [@DeMicheli1994SynthesisOptimization; @Izraelevitz2017Chisel], yet engineers working through any abstraction still need to challenge the problem formulation, inspect decisive failure traces, and recognize physical effects the model omits. As automated loops absorb routine microarchitectural sweeps and propose broader redesigns, that diagnostic access is how architects identify missing constraints, develop cross-layer alternatives, and judge whether the combined evidence supports a system recommendation.

The same delegation creates an apprenticeship risk. Junior engineers who encounter designs only through prompts and scorecards may never build the diagnostic experience needed to challenge a result or recommend a consequential change. Training curricula must therefore give them deliberate opportunities to investigate failures (@sec-curriculum-certification).

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Judgment precedes and governs automation"}
**The principle:** Automation may formulate problems, explore alternatives, implement designs, and analyze systems. Architects must retain the technical understanding needed to challenge and revise the problem, the abstraction, and the system boundaries as results emerge.

**The application:** A review supporting a commitment should explain how the component results support one feasible system recommendation and what evidence could overturn it. It should identify the architect responsible for that recommendation and the commitment authority responsible for the organizational decision.
:::

## Framing Cross-Layer Problems {#sec-framing-architecture-problem}

If an architect gives an automated optimizer a narrow, single-layer objective such as maximizing neural processing unit (NPU) matrix-array utilization, the search can return a configuration that wins on that metric and fails as a system. Its bursty direct memory access (DMA) traffic can saturate the LPDDR5 memory bus, starve the host CPU, and push package power past 3\ W. The architect's judgment therefore enters first in framing the problem that an automated design loop will explore. The architect defines the system boundary, identifies the governing cross-layer interactions, decides which physical consequences the evaluation must measure, and revisits those choices when generated candidates and tool runs reveal missing constraints or better organizations. The choice of mechanisms, interfaces, and fallback strategies frames the design space itself [@PattersonDitzel1980RISC], so the architect's role extends beyond bounding the physical hardware. The architect also designs the decision workflow: which methods propose candidate modifications, which modeling tools estimate their properties, which validation checks screen candidates, and how the team investigates cross-layer disagreements.

In @sec-intent-vs-spec, we decomposed the Lighthouse extended-reality (XR) specification request, "Design a low-power, 64-bit RISC-V-based compute subsystem for a real-time mobile XR workload," across eight requirement domains. Consider a candidate organization that combines a host CPU with an NPU across a UCIe packaging link. That template is one possible organization rather than a choice settled by the request, and how deeply the team must evaluate it depends on the commitment at stake.

A freeze decision asks far more of the requirement decomposition than a local exploration does. Studying array utilization requires only cycle-level modeling and mapping search, whereas freezing that array alongside its software interface and packaging link demands evidence that the selected parts work together as a subsystem. Before recommending a freeze, the architect must trace how compiler lowering through Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) shapes the memory traffic. The architect must then check whether the resulting execution meets timing and stays within the total 3\ W subsystem thermal design power (TDP) limit. While IP review and non-recurring engineering (NRE) capital review add organizational conditions for proceeding, the specific architecture question determines which technical models and checks must run to support the recommendation.

Across decisions of this kind, eight recurring judgments help turn isolated tool results into one coherent recommendation (@tbl-architect-technical-judgments). Together they let the architect surface missing constraints, resolve cross-layer trade-offs, and state residual risk plainly. The commitment decision then rests on a physically grounded account of the system and its remaining uncertainties.

| **Judgment** | **Architectural question** | **Lighthouse consequence** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Problem choice and reframing** | Is the stated problem still the one the product needs solved? | Deciding whether the goal is maximizing raw NPU general matrix multiply (GEMM) utilization or meeting the proposed 120\ frames per second (FPS) mobile XR operating point and its workload-specific deadlines within a 3\ W TDP envelope. |
| **Abstraction** | Which details can be simplified for this decision? | A cycle-level NPU model can compare matrix mappings locally, but it cannot hide Triton/LLVM/MLIR compiler lowering, static random-access memory (SRAM) / LPDDR5 memory traffic, UCIe interconnect energy, physical timing, or the 3\ W subsystem boundary from a freeze decision. |
| **System boundary** | Where do workload, software, hardware, package, physical design, and product effects meet? | Deciding whether NPU array sizing can be analyzed in isolation, or must encompass host 64-bit RISC-V application core with vector extensions (RV64GCV) task dispatch, UCIe chiplet routing, dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) bandwidth contention, and packaging thermal limits. |
| **Architecture synthesis** | Do chosen mechanisms, interfaces, software paths, and implementation choices form one feasible system? | Confirming that the NPU matrix engine, RV64GCV CPU contract, compiler lowering pipeline, LPDDR5 memory subsystem, and firmware fallback paths form a coherent, manufacturable subsystem. |
| **Missing constraints** | What has the formulation, representation, or tool path left out? | Uncovering omitted physical and legal factors: transient power delivery network (PDN) voltage droop ($di/dt$), 3\ W thermal dissipation limits, UCIe signal integrity, IP indemnification, and hardware chicken-bit fallbacks. |
| **Cross-layer trade-off** | Which feasible point best serves the product when objectives conflict? | Resolving the tension between host RV64GCV vector tail latency, NPU matrix throughput, LPDDR5 memory power, UCIe die-to-die routing congestion, and manual review burden. |
| **Mechanism and consequence** | Does the proposed explanation fit the observations, and what happens if it is wrong? | Evaluating whether an apparent speedup is driven by architectural dataflow or an unmodeled memory wait state, where an erroneous tapeout freeze risks multimillion-dollar silicon mask respins. |
| **Commitment under uncertainty** | Are remaining risks understood, containable, and worth accepting? | Recommending against physical tapeout when static timing closure, formal property bounds, IP indemnification, and power delivery margins remain uncharacterized. |
: **Architecture judgment gives technical work its system meaning.** Architects choose the question, abstraction, boundary, and consequence before the commitment authority decides whether the design advances. {#tbl-architect-technical-judgments tbl-colwidths="[22,38,40]"}

In practice, these eight judgments expose where a feasibility claim rests on physical coupling that individual models left out. In our hypothetical CPU-NPU-UCIe candidate, the team does not yet know whether NPU DMA burst sizing, LPDDR5 bus contention, host CPU interrupt latency, and package thermal gradients allow a 120\ FPS XR rendering target inside a 3\ W thermal envelope. That is an open question to investigate, not a demonstrated property of a feasible subsystem. Because simplified abstractions routinely hide bottlenecks that cross block boundaries, identifying those interactions early tells the architect which models are safe to trust and which additional implementation checks the recommendation needs.

## Selecting System Abstractions and Bounds {#sec-selecting-abstractions-constraints}

Once the system boundaries are set, the architect chooses the representations and analytical models that govern exploration, because every architectural model is defined as much by what it omits as by what it represents. While a memory trace in Ramulator can expose channel contention and an NPU dataflow model in SCALE-Sim shows how a mapping occupies the array, neither view alone establishes physical timing or thermal feasibility. Moving to RTL simulation, physical implementation tools, and a package thermal model adds those physical observations, but it also creates a reconciliation problem because the workload, interfaces, and operating conditions must agree across every view. When the architect selects an abstraction, the task therefore includes naming the omitted details that could flip the decision and scheduling a check that can observe them.

::: {.column-margin}
**Architecture description standards.** The International Organization for Standardization, International Electrotechnical Commission, and Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (ISO/IEC/IEEE) 42010 standard distinguishes an entity architecture from an architecture description that expresses it. The standard specifies requirements for architecture viewpoints and model kinds, but it does not prescribe this book's chapter structure, a team's specific design process, or the organizational assignment of commitment authority [@ISOIECIEEE2022ArchitectureDescription].
:::

Choosing an abstraction also fixes what architectural state each predictor, generator, optimizer, or tool is allowed to modify and which measurements constrain those edits. Consider a learned macro placer such as AlphaChip [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement]. If a team configured a hypothetical NPU placement objective that omitted power delivery network (PDN) and package-thermal effects, the optimizer could cluster high-activity vector units where transient supply droop threatens timing, or return a layout that exceeds the combined package's thermal limit. Neither effect would lower its placement score. Those physical consequences require separate checks, not because of any reported failure in AlphaChip itself, but because the objective function never measured them. A generator given direct control over standard-cell placement likewise requires checks for foundry design rules, well spacing, and available routing tracks. Across both macro and standard-cell flows, the architect defines block boundaries, curates macro sets, sets timing and power constraints across host CPU and NPU cores, chooses comparison baselines, and arranges physical signoff.

The permitted changes can also limit a search even when the relevant constraint is known. When an optimizer is confined to a fixed template and none of its permitted parameter choices relieves a saturated memory interface, the search stalls at that template's boundary. Authorizing a different organization expands the design possibilities, but also requires representations and checks that cover its new interfaces and physical effects. The architect must establish that scope before relying on the redesigned system.

Beyond choosing models for individual tools, architects govern how components interact by defining interface contracts, assigning revision authority, selecting independent signoff checks, and auditing shared assumptions across verification steps. Many consequential constraints originate as unwritten engineering experience [@Polanyi1966TacitDimension, p. 4]: compiler leads may know that a proposed matrix opcode lacks an efficient lowering path, while physical-design leads recognize power-grid heuristics that break down on dense CPU-NPU floorplans. Language models can help locate, compare, and organize these scattered expert judgments for formal review. Any constraint that shapes the design, however, still requires verification checks matched to its risk and scope, whether automated checkers, conventional EDA tools, domain specialists, or peer reviewers run them.

Once the team accepts such a constraint, the architectural record should state its source, its scope, the interfaces it affects, its known conflicts, and the conditions that would reopen it. Suppose a physical designer's rule bars placing two high-current macros on the same power stripe for a given metal stack and operating threshold. The architect decides how to enforce that rule in the floorplanner and evaluates the resulting routing overhead. If the project later moves to a new power-grid template or a 3D stacked die, the physical assumptions behind that rule no longer hold, which triggers a fresh review rather than leaving an obsolete restriction in force. Recording the constraint together with its operating assumptions keeps an optimizer from quietly violating an unwritten physical limit, yet lets the team retire that limit when the technology changes instead of rejecting valid designs. Even well-chosen models and constraints, however, evaluate only one view of the hardware at a time; the architect still has to integrate their separate outputs into a single working system.

## Governing System Integration {#sec-orchestrating-system-integration}

A design candidate becomes a viable architecture, rather than an assortment of isolated optimizations, only when its mechanisms and interfaces hold together under the physical and logical conditions of the full stack. Automated methods can reason across layers when those interactions are represented and checked, but any result from a tool or domain specialist covers only the interactions its model includes. An NPU array optimization that omits host CPU cache coherence, memory channel contention, or UCIe chiplet thermal dissipation cannot establish feasibility across those boundaries. The architect has to set and challenge the scope of those studies, expose missing interactions, and compose specialized results into a unified system recommendation.

Consider a hypothetical revision of the Lighthouse XR system-on-chip (SoC). Trace analyses in gem5 and SCALE-Sim support the target frame rate, MLIR compiler searches yield legal NPU tiling, Verilator RTL simulations pass, Ramulator memory models satisfy local bandwidth checks, OpenSTA reports that timing constraints are met, and power-aware checks using Unified Power Format (UPF) verify the declared power-gating behavior. Each check passes in isolation, yet combining the results exposes two cross-layer faults. The burst memory traffic introduced by the new NPU tiling pushes estimated subsystem power across SRAM arrays, UCIe links, and LPDDR5 channels past the 3\ W thermal envelope, and a critical tail-latency path has no software fallback.

To resolve those faults, the architect proposes coordinated adjustments across the stack: assigning tail-latency handling to the host CPU core, narrowing NPU DMA bursts, rebalancing memory buffers, and specifying firmware fallback paths. Each adjustment creates a new cross-layer obligation of its own. Narrower bursts relieve memory contention at the expense of accelerator throughput and must be re-evaluated against the frame deadline; moving work to the host CPU requires checking its scheduling and power draw under concurrent load; and rebalancing buffers requires checking capacity and backpressure under the revised traffic pattern. The firmware fallback path must likewise preserve functional correctness, with its latency and power costs measured under the conditions in which it runs. A different kind of fallback, programmable control-register overrides (often called *chicken-bits*), offers a post-silicon way to disable a faulty speculative path, but only if verification proves that flipping the override actually contains the fault. Working through these coupled checks turns a collection of local passes into a candidate system whose end-to-end interactions can be tested.

The resulting recommendation explains why the revised subsystem should meet its requirements and identifies any checks that still disagree. Those remaining disagreements deserve close attention before a preferred candidate advances, because they often expose a broken interface assumption that no single-domain optimization examined.

## Resolving Cross-Layer Discrepancies {#sec-resolving-discrepancies}

When models across different domains disagree, the conflict may expose incompatible assumptions, competing approximations, or a candidate that genuinely improves one metric while failing another requirement. If a cycle-level simulator reports performance gains for a new NPU array mapping while physical signoff tools report power-grid voltage droop under concurrent host CPU vector loads, both tools may be right, and the faster mapping is still infeasible under realistic system load. The architect cannot average those metrics, nor, under schedule pressure, pick the more convenient report to dismiss a blocking failure. Architectural judgment begins instead by asking what each result actually establishes. Before the design can advance, the team must explain the physical mechanism behind the conflict, reexamine the model abstractions, run a check that separates the competing explanations, or hold the candidate until the blocking discrepancy is resolved.

Three steps help separate a candidate defect from a disagreement about what the tools checked:

1. **Contract and condition alignment**: The architect and domain specialists identify the requirement each check addresses and compare implementation versions, workloads, operating conditions, and assumptions. Because checks of different requirements need not agree on whether a candidate is favorable, a valid failure of an applicable blocking requirement rules out the candidate under those conditions even when another check passes.
2. **Abstraction correction**: When checks encode inconsistent assumptions or interfaces, the team determines which representation departs from the intended product contract, corrects the erroneous abstraction, model, or interface definition, and reruns the affected tool paths. If the contract itself is ambiguous, the architect resolves its meaning against the product requirements before rerunning the checks rather than weakening a valid requirement to obtain a pass.
3. **Investigation of unresolved discrepancies**: When formal proofs and cycle-accurate models still disagree about an interface invariant, the team selects an observation that can distinguish the competing explanations. If the discrepancy cannot be resolved within verification budgets, the candidate remains blocked from advancing past the affected check, and the architect and affected specialists record what remains unexplained before signoff.

Suppose a coherence verifier using SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) and bounded model checking (BMC) returns a counterexample within $k = 50$ cycles against a blocking property between host CPU caches and NPU DMA stores.[^fn-bmc-c11] A high-level software model, meanwhile, treats the same execution as legal under high-contention LPDDR5 traffic. Neither the architect nor an automated loop may weaken the property, discard the failing workload, or relabel the counterexample as passing. To resolve the conflict between the formal check and the software model, we ask whether both tools encode the same product contract and permit the memory events in the counterexample. Tracing how the software model represents those exact memory events locates where the two views diverge. If the counterexample reflects behavior the candidate hardware can produce and violates a valid blocking requirement, the candidate fails; otherwise, the team corrects the erroneous representation or resolves the contract ambiguity and reruns both paths.

That resolution assumes the property itself is correct, which no longer holds automatically when generative models propose both the candidate RTL and the formal assertions. Verification engineers must then check the blocking assertions against the product contract independently of the generated RTL. Mutation testing can measure the harness's sensitivity to injected faults, but cannot rule out specification omissions shared by the candidate and its checkers.

[^fn-bmc-c11]: **Bounded model checking and SystemVerilog Assertions**: SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) express formal properties to check. Bounded model checking (BMC) searches for a property violation within a specified number of unrolled execution cycles under encoded assumptions; a completed passing check establishes the absence of a counterexample within that finite bound, not an inductive proof at arbitrary depth [@SymbiYosys].

A different discrepancy arises when feasible candidates pass their blocking checks but return overlapping estimates for tail latency and subsystem power. Here the architect asks whether workload sampling, model error, or untested operating corners could flip which design wins. The right response is to run the least costly check with enough fidelity to separate the candidates on the specific uncertainty that could change the recommendation: matched cycle-level trace runs in gem5 for workload-dependent timing, physical thermal simulations for heat buildup, OpenSTA static timing runs for path slack, or post-layout power-grid analyses for voltage droop. If the available checks cannot resolve the overlap within budget, the architect keeps the recommendation narrow and favors choices that remain reversible. Once these discrepancies and uncertainties are resolved or explicitly bounded, the architect has a qualified hardware recommendation, which raises the separate governance question of what that evidence actually authorizes.

## Separating Evidence from Commitments {#sec-linking-results-claims-commitments}

A sound hardware candidate does not by itself establish that an AI-native workflow outperformed a conventional baseline, a workflow advantage does not prove that its candidate meets product requirements, and neither finding constitutes a decision to tape out silicon.

The architect connects hardware evidence to project governance through the recommendation. It presents the preferred candidate alongside evaluated alternatives, explains the cross-layer trade-offs, documents boundary conditions and signoff checks, and states the remaining uncertainties. Domain specialists remain responsible for the validity and scope of their signoffs across timing closure, power integrity, physical implementation, and reliability. The organization decides whether the supported recommendation justifies the next commitment.

Among the three meanings of progress in @sec-moonshot, methodological value and the commitment decision require independent judgments:

1. **Methodological value (program claim)**: Did the complete approach improve the architecture result or reduce total cost to reach a comparable result? (Classified as *supported*, *unsupported*, or *unresolved*.)
2. **Commitment decision (architecture commitment)**: Do the people authorized to commit the project, weighing the architectural recommendation, trade-offs, result limits, and residual risk, decide that the work justifies the next transition?

Keeping these judgments separate protects each decision from the other, in both directions. Even when a workflow claim is *supported*, a faster search or a better Pareto frontier does not compel a silicon commitment if physical thermals, organizational capacity, or business risks remain unacceptable. Conversely, an *unresolved* workflow comparison does not prevent an organization from committing to a sound hardware architecture backed by thorough physical signoff. Because an evidence status never records a product decision, every recommendation must identify who is authorized to approve the next transition and present the specific hardware evidence that transition requires.

## Governing Tapeout Commitments {#sec-governing-tapeout-commitments}

What a commitment requires depends on how much of the design the next transition locks in. Moving from high-level exploration toward physical silicon progressively freezes interfaces, bus contracts, and floorplans. Early in the design cycle, changing ISA extensions or buffer layouts means editing software models or RTL. After freeze, changing package substrate routing or reticle masks can cost millions of dollars and months of delay [@Patel2022MaskSetCosts]. The supporting evidence must therefore address the consequences that will become hardest to reverse.

::: {.callout-war-story title="An architecture can outlast its original product plan"}
**The claim.** Larrabee described a many-core x86 architecture for visual computing, with wide vector units, coherent caches, and a software renderer in place of most fixed-function graphics hardware [@SeilerEtAl2008Larrabee]. In September 2009, Intel demonstrated Larrabee silicon and described plans for discrete graphics products [@Intel2009LarrabeeDemonstration].

**The gap.** In May 2010, Intel announced Many Integrated Core product plans targeting high-performance computing and identified Larrabee as one of the projects from which the architecture was derived [@Intel2010MICPlans]. This chronology establishes architectural reuse under a different product plan. It does not disclose the complete internal evidence or capital-allocation rationale behind that plan.

**The lesson.** Reusing an architecture and committing to a particular product are different decisions. A recommendation must identify the target workload, product requirements, and remaining expenditure for the proposed transition. The people responsible for that product must decide whether to proceed; a published architecture or a working demonstration cannot supply that decision.
:::

Execution rights can extend to rewriting interfaces, pipelines, and compiler passes, but still stop short of commitment. A generator with the authority to rewrite RTL across modules does not thereby gain authority to approve timing waivers, relax signoff constraints, or declare its own output tapeout-ready.

Separating execution from commitment requires a clear record of who decides what. Commitment records specify which design advances, which alternatives were rejected, which conditions the evidence covered, what uncertainty remains, and what triggers would reopen the choice. The division in @tbl-lighthouse-action-rights makes three responsibilities explicit: doing the design work, establishing what its results support, and deciding whether to commit. These responsibilities may involve overlapping teams, but completing one step never authorizes the next.

| **Decision** | **Technical question** | **Boundary** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Execute design work** | What candidate state may this person, model, or tool change, and when must it stop? | Work stays within the declared design space, interfaces, budget, and evaluator boundary. |
| **Establish what a result supports** | What does this check show about this artifact under these conditions and assumptions? | Domain specialists own result validity and domain scope. The architect determines how that result applies to the system decision. |
| **Commit the architecture** | Does the integrated design justify the next consequential transition (e.g., tapeout freeze)? | The named commitment authority decides after considering the architect's system recommendation, alternatives, cross-layer results, specialist concurrences, uncertainty, and residual risk. |
: **Execution, support, and commitment carry different responsibilities.** A successful tool run or a favorable local result cannot silently authorize a system architecture. {#tbl-lighthouse-action-rights tbl-colwidths="[28,34,38]"}

The table applies a distinction from classic human-automation frameworks, which separate information acquisition, analysis, decision selection, and action implementation [@ParasuramanEtAl2000LevelsAutomation]. In a hardware project, that distinction determines who may advance a candidate and on what basis.[^fn-kernel-maintainer-c11] Once domain specialists sign off on their checks, those findings enter the architect's recommendation, and the named authority records a decision against that recommendation while the underlying check records remain immutable.

[^fn-kernel-maintainer-c11]: **Linux kernel review as a limited analogy**: Kernel submission guidance separates submission to the relevant maintainers, review, testing, and the Developer Certificate of Origin; `Signed-off-by:` records the contributor's certification of the right to submit or pass on the patch, not proof that it is correct [@LinuxKernelSubmittingPatches]. The useful parallel is separating a candidate proposal from its review and acceptance, not equating a maintainer's role or that contributor declaration with hardware signoff or tapeout responsibility.

That immutability matters when operating conditions shift or new physical constraints emerge and make earlier results inapplicable. Rather than overwriting old measurements, the team appends fresh checks with their conditions and versions to preserve the basis of the original decision for later diagnosis. An intact record makes that history inspectable, even though it cannot by itself prove that the original checks were sufficient or their assumptions correct. Before a named authority approves a tapeout freeze on the basis of that record, the review must clear three concrete obligations: intellectual-property provenance, containment of residual technical risk, and capital and physical qualification.

### IP Provenance and Indemnification

When an automated generator emits large spans of RTL or millions of netlist lines, structural refactoring, signal renaming, and logic synthesis can disguise memorized third-party or copylefted source logic from simple token scanners. An unguarded prompt can also leak proprietary foundry process design kit (PDK) rules to an external model endpoint. Before committing capital to silicon fabrication, the organization must therefore resolve the IP conditions under which it can use the candidate. For generated RTL, the technical record should identify the supplied sources, permitted transformations, and checks performed. It should also expose what is unknown about the generator's training data or the origin of an emitted fragment, so that those limits stay visible to the responsible IP reviewers.

How deep those provenance checks must go depends on the scope of generation. Engineers can review a generated leaf module line by line and scan it for token-level similarity. Swept values such as cache depths carry little copyright risk of their own, so legal review shifts to the data used to train performance surrogates. Once an autonomous design system synthesizes multi-tier microarchitectural logic across blocks, however, visual inspection can no longer detect semantic memorization or copyright infringement. The engineering organization then surrounds the design system with four complementary governance controls:

- **Prompt and lineage records**: Retain the supplied specifications, prompts, model checkpoints, random seeds, tool transcripts, and intermediate artifacts with version identities and integrity hashes. A hash such as SHA-256 detects whether an artifact changed, and a digital signature authenticates its signer, but neither establishes where an emitted fragment originated. Restricting retrieval to approved specifications likewise limits the supplied context, and formal equivalence checking can establish correspondence to a reference under declared assumptions, yet neither proves training-data provenance or noninfringement.
- **Similarity and license screening**: Screen generated RTL for recognizable overlap with indexed source repositories and retain the findings for review. A clean scan covers only the sources and similarities the scanner can detect; it is not an origin guarantee.
- **Restricted processing environments**: Declare where foundry PDK rules, cell libraries, third-party commercial IP, and internal protocols may be processed so that restricted materials stay out of training corpora and external model contexts. Restrict tool and network access accordingly, and retain the execution and transfer records needed to check compliance with that boundary.
- **Third-party IP boundaries**: Pin vendor block versions and interface contracts, and limit automated modifications to the scope the organization has authorized. Where internals are unavailable or modification is prohibited, explore integration through the exposed interfaces. Boundary checks can reveal prohibited tool actions without establishing the full legal status of the resulting system.

Together, these controls make the technical history reviewable, though IP acceptance and any indemnification decision still require the organization's separate review rather than following from passing functional checks.

### Managing Residual Risk with Hardware Chicken-Bits

Some uncertainties remain when a design approaches freeze. A hardware chicken-bit selects an implemented fallback mode through a privileged control register, allowing firmware to disable a risky optimization after fabrication. The existence of the register does not establish that the fallback contains the fault or preserves the product's requirements. Verification must exercise its nominal and asserted states, including the implemented control path. Otherwise, a fallback branch tied to a constant during synthesis may disappear through constant propagation and dead-code elimination.

Consider a proposed Lighthouse control that staggers activation across NPU multiply-accumulate columns. Simultaneous activation could create a rapid current transient ($di/dt$) and supply-voltage droop that threatens setup timing.[^fn-di-dt-c11] Staggering activation might reduce that transient, but could also lower throughput enough to miss the frame deadline. This example is constructed; no such control has been implemented or measured in the retained study.

A residual-risk statement must connect the failure mode, its consequence, the remaining uncertainty, a detecting check, and any containment action. Here, the mode is voltage droop during burst activation; the consequences include corrupted computation or throttling below the proposed 120\ FPS operating point. Dynamic power-integrity analysis under declared activity and package assumptions would test the droop mechanism, while post-silicon monitors could help detect it if their sensitivity were established. Until those checks run, neither the droop bound nor the proposed control's effectiveness is known. The recommendation must state that gap rather than count the proposed control as protection.

[^fn-di-dt-c11]: **Inductive voltage droop and current transients**: Inductive voltage droop ($V = L \cdot di/dt$) occurs across package and on-chip power distribution inductances when clock gating or simultaneous transistor switching causes rapid changes in current ($di/dt$). The resulting voltage decrease can threaten SRAM state retention or logic timing.

A commitment record should state the performance penalty of any fallback it relies on. For latency, a *derating penalty* compares nominal and derated execution under the same workload and operating conditions:[^fn-derating-penalty-c11]

$$
\Delta_{\text{derate}} = \frac{T_{\text{derated}} - T_{\text{nominal}}}{T_{\text{nominal}}}
$$

Here $T_{\text{nominal}}$ and $T_{\text{derated}}$ are the execution times with the ordinary and fallback behavior. For the proposed staggered activation, this penalty remains unmeasured. The fallback must still meet the frame deadline and 3\ W subsystem budget under the conditions in which the team intends to rely on it.

Other fallbacks can change that assessment. If a cache control simultaneously forces write-through operation, its extra memory traffic could alter power and latency while the NPU runs in the derated mode. Verification must cover the legal combinations and their system interactions, not only each control in isolation. Hierarchical proofs can help when their composition assumptions hold; pairwise checks alone do not establish global deadlock freedom. The control path must also remain usable under the fault it is meant to contain.

[^fn-derating-penalty-c11]: **Microarchitectural derating penalty**: Silicon practitioners introduce derating factors to penalize nominal performance estimates when post-silicon workarounds (such as serialization or wait states) must be engaged to avoid physical timing violations, dynamic voltage droop, or race conditions under worst-case thermal and voltage corners.

Even a passing derated check would establish only that the declared fallback stays within the requirements and conditions actually tested, not that the product is commercially viable or insulated from financial risk. The architect records that technical limit so the named commitment authority can decide whether the remaining risk justifies tapeout.

Shipping an uncharacterized feature disabled by default creates a related obligation. Its disabled state must preserve baseline requirements, its enable path must stay restricted to authorized modes, and reset and fault handling must maintain that separation. The exception needs an owner and a review trigger tied to characterization. Otherwise, temporary exceptions can become accepted practice without the evidence originally required [@Vaughan1996Challenger].

Automated exploration may investigate relaxed constraints in an isolated workspace, but the responsible specialists must approve any change to release constraints or waivers. The record preserves the technical justification, affected conditions, checks, and reconsideration trigger; a signature identifies the approver without proving the exception sound. If a risk remains unacceptable and no verified avoidance or containment exists, the candidate cannot advance. Accepting a risk without containment requires an explicit rationale from the responsible authority.

### Capital Allocation and Physical Qualification

```{python}
#| echo: false
# Errata study: every number in this section is read from the committed data in
# data/studies/01-silicon-errata-archaeology/ (errata_classified.csv, sources.csv,
# audit_metrics.json). Reproduce with the commands in that folder's README.
import csv
import json
from pathlib import Path

import _python.plots as _ap

_errata_dir = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2] / "data/studies/01-silicon-errata-archaeology"
_errata = list(csv.DictReader((_errata_dir / "errata_classified.csv").open(encoding="utf-8")))
_sources = list(csv.DictReader(
    line for line in (_errata_dir / "sources.csv").open(encoding="utf-8") if not line.startswith("#")
))
_audit = json.loads((_errata_dir / "audit_metrics.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
_words = "zero one two three four five six seven eight nine ten eleven twelve".split()


def _pct(x):
    return f"{100 * x:.0f}"


def _ci(pair):
    return f"{100 * pair[0]:.0f} to {100 * pair[1]:.0f}"


errata_n = f"{len(_errata):,}"
families_n = len(_sources)
intel_families = sum(r["vendor"] == "Intel" for r in _sources)
amd_families = families_n - intel_families
audited_n = _audit["audited"]
agree_pct = _pct(_audit["agreement_weighted"])
agree_ci = _ci(_audit["agreement_weighted_ci95"])
_sh = _audit["shares"]
_mem = _sh["Memory controller, coherence fabric, and I/O"]
mem_adj, mem_ci = _pct(_mem["adjusted_share"]), _ci(_mem["adjusted_ci95"])
arith_n = _words[_audit["arithmetic_datapath_audited"]]
no_fix_pct = _pct(_audit["status_counts"]["No Fix"] / len(_errata))

# Composition of the largest reporting class, by rule label.
_by_rule = {}
for _r in _errata:
    _by_rule[_r["subsystem"]] = _by_rule.get(_r["subsystem"], 0) + 1
_io = _by_rule["I/O and peripheral interfaces"]
_mc = _by_rule["Memory controller and DRAM"]
_coh = _by_rule["Coherence and on-die or socket fabric"]
io_of_class_pct = _pct(_io / (_io + _mc + _coh))
memsys_rule_pct = f"{100 * (_mc + _coh + _by_rule['Caches, TLBs, and load-store ordering']) / len(_errata):.1f}"

_s18_sum = json.loads((_errata_dir.parent / "18-errata-by-year" / "summary.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
launch_yr_min, launch_yr_max = _s18_sum["launch_year_range"]

```

Advancing from simulation to silicon commits NRE capital for mask tooling and physical qualification.[^fn-mask-nre-c11] Faster candidate generation does not reduce the mask charge for a chosen process or remove the cost of containing defects after fabrication. Published processor errata make that continuing obligation concrete. Our retained analysis covers `{python} errata_n` itemized errata across `{python} families_n` CPU families (`{python} intel_families` from Intel and `{python} amd_families` from AMD) introduced between `{python} launch_yr_min` and `{python} launch_yr_max` [@Intel2022XeonE5v4SpecUpdate; @Intel2020XeonScalableSpecUpdate; @Intel2023XeonScalableGen2SpecUpdate; @Intel2026XeonScalableGen3SpecUpdate; @Intel2026XeonScalableGen4SpecUpdate; @Intel2026XeonScalableGen5SpecUpdate; @Intel2025Core8th9thGenSpecUpdate; @Intel2026Core10thGenSpecUpdate; @Intel2026Core11thGenTigerLakeSpecUpdate; @Intel2023Core11thGenRocketLakeSpecUpdate; @Intel2026Core12thGenSpecUpdate; @Intel2026Core13th14thGenSpecUpdate; @Intel2026CoreUltraSpecUpdate; @Intel2026CoreUltra200VSpecUpdate; @Intel2026CoreUltraSeries2SpecUpdate; @AMD2023Family17h00hRevisionGuide; @AMD2026Family17h30hRevisionGuide; @AMD2025Family19h10hRevisionGuide; @AMD2025Family1Ah00hRevisionGuide]. The extracted entries match each document's summary table.

[^fn-mask-nre-c11]: **Mask tooling non-recurring engineering and physical signoff**: A reticle mask set is an upfront capital expenditure, with one photomask for each patterned layer, paid before any production wafer is processed. One analyst estimate puts a mask set above \$1 million at 28\ nm, above \$10 million at 7\ nm, and near \$40 million approaching 3\ nm [@Patel2022MaskSetCosts]. A respin that changes many layers incurs much of this charge again, along with months of fabrication delay.

Memory controllers, coherence fabrics, and caches admit many interleavings of concurrent requests, so their large verification state spaces might lead us to expect a concentration of published defects there. Arithmetic units, with comparatively compact specifications and mature formal checks, might appear less exposed. Subsystem counts let us examine that expectation descriptively, though they do not measure verification difficulty or defect probability.

Our classification uses retained keyword rules and a model-assisted audit of a stratified sample of `{python} audited_n` errata (@fig-errata-subsystem-shares). The rule labels agree with that reading on an estimated `{python} agree_pct`% of the corpus (95% interval `{python} agree_ci`%). Classes that failed the audit were merged with adjacent classes or folded into the unclassified group. Because the same model family helped draft the rules and label the sample, the adjusted shares are not independently verified ground truth.[^fn-errata-audit-c11]

[^fn-errata-audit-c11]: **Errata classification audit**: Hiding the rule labels from the audit worksheet does not remove assumptions shared by model-assisted rules and labels. An independent human relabeling of the stratified sample, blind to both sets of labels, has not been performed. The retained study includes the rules, sample, class consolidations, and adjusted estimates.

![**Published CPU errata spread across subsystems; no reported class holds much more than a fifth.** Shares of `{python} errata_n` errata from the specification updates and revision guides of `{python} families_n` Intel and AMD CPU families, grouped by committed keyword rules into six reported classes. The largest class is mostly I/O and peripheral errata. Bars give the rule-assigned share; dots and whiskers give the share adjusted by a model-assisted audit of a stratified sample of `{python} audited_n` errata, with 95% intervals. The hatched bar holds errata that no rule matched and two classes that failed the audit.](images/fig-errata-subsystem-shares){#fig-errata-subsystem-shares width="100%" fig-alt="Horizontal bar chart of published CPU errata shares for six subsystem classes and a hatched bar for errata not resolved to a class. I/O with memory controllers and coherence, debug and performance monitoring, and core execution with caches and translation lookaside buffers have bars of similar length, virtualization and security is somewhat shorter, and power and interrupts are the shortest. Each bar carries a dot with an interval marking an audit-adjusted estimate that overlaps the bars of neighboring classes."}

The largest reported class by rule-assigned share combines I/O and peripheral interfaces with memory controllers and coherence fabrics; its estimated share after the audit is `{python} mem_adj`% (95% interval `{python} mem_ci`%). Yet `{python} io_of_class_pct`% of that class's rule-assigned entries concern I/O and peripherals. Memory controllers, coherence fabrics, and caches together account for `{python} memsys_rule_pct`% of the corpus by rule; they do not dominate it. Core execution, caches, and translation lookaside buffers (TLBs) form one class of comparable share, and the debug and monitoring logic that observes execution forms another. Arithmetic datapath defects are uncommon in the audit sample: `{python} arith_n` of `{python} audited_n` entries describe a floating-point, integer, or vector unit that computes or schedules incorrectly. Many documented behaviors instead concern control and integration. A virtual-machine entry that clears the trace-enable bit can emit a spurious trace packet [@Intel2020XeonScalableSpecUpdate], and after a C6 sleep-state exit the processor can dispatch a queued interrupt before an earlier one of the same priority completes [@Intel2022XeonE5v4SpecUpdate].

These shares describe customer-facing documents, not a complete census of defects. They lack denominators for subsystem size or complexity, use classes of unequal scope, and draw mostly on Intel documents. Erratum titles also recur across processor families, but matching wording does not establish identical hardware root causes. Counting distinct titles changes the shares without making memory-system defects dominant. The counts therefore cannot establish escape rates or test the state-space explanation. They do show why ownership must extend across power-state transitions, interrupts, isolation, interfaces, and diagnostic logic, rather than end at a correctly computed arithmetic result.

The documents also record whether a fix is planned or has been made, and `{python} no_fix_pct`% of the corpus carries no planned fix. The study retains the least resolved disposition when steppings differ, so this percentage describes entries across the covered variants, not the fraction of shipped processors with an active defect or the availability of a workaround. Any workaround relied on in a commitment still needs functional checks and measured costs under its intended conditions.

These findings do not compare generated RTL with human-written RTL. They identify behaviors an AI-native design system must address if it generates control and integration logic, and responsibilities its architect must carry into commitment review. The complete workflow comparison must count the effort of checking those control and integration behaviors (@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect). The product decision separately weighs physical readiness, remaining expenditure, shipment volume, and residual risk (@sec-design-cost-pressure).

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="The Lighthouse commitment remains open"}
**Context.** Freezing a Level-2 cache capacity or selecting an accelerator organization for the Lighthouse mobile XR subsystem would constrain later software, memory, and physical implementation choices.

**Application.** Before such a freeze, the architect must establish that the selected organization meets its workload requirements within the subsystem's memory, power, and physical constraints. The required physical signoff, power modeling, and system-level checks remain missing.

**Outcome.** The supported recommendation is to obtain the missing system evidence before advancing toward freeze or tapeout. The person responsible for the product would still need to assess the resulting recommendation across all eight requirement domains (@sec-intent-vs-spec) and record a decision.
:::

The verification plan must connect each required property to qualified specialist evidence (@sec-mapping-requirements-toolchains), including implementation correspondence, physical timing, power and package behavior, and manufacturing test readiness where the transition requires them. The architect integrates those signoffs and their exceptions into the recommendation; the organization separately resolves rights to use the design and the remaining product risks. Missing required evidence prevents advancement, while an eligible design still requires an authorized decision.

## Sustaining Architectural Ownership {#sec-sustaining-responsibility}

Architectural ownership continues as teams integrate revisions and as deployed silicon encounters new conditions. It requires access to the specifications, models, traces, signoff reports, and rejected alternatives needed to investigate a recommendation, together with authority to stop or reopen it. Naming a reviewer without that access or authority creates the mismatch between responsibility and control that Elish calls a *moral crumple zone*.[^fn-crumple-c11] Research on automation bias likewise warns against substituting an automated recommendation for independent examination [@SkitkaEtAl1999AutomationBias].

[^fn-crumple-c11]: **Moral crumple zones**: Elish's term for human operators who bear responsibility for an automated system's failure despite having limited control over its autonomous behavior [@Elish2019MoralCrumpleZones]. It describes an organizational mismatch between responsibility and operational control, not a rule assigning legal liability.

### Keeping Recommendations Valid During Integration {#sec-sustaining-alignment-churn}

An architectural recommendation can become stale before silicon reaches the foundry. Engineers and automated loops change RTL, device drivers, compiler backends, and firmware while the project is under evaluation. The architect ties each recommendation to an integration snapshot and states which changes require fresh checks. Delegated subblock optimization also needs explicit boundaries for external protocols, clock crossings, and register maps.

Continuous integration runs equivalence, timing, and interface checks at a fidelity matched to the changed artifacts; full physical qualification covers the integrated candidate proposed for commitment. A local change that preserves its source-level interface can still alter cross-block timing or power, so a clean merge does not establish that the earlier recommendation remains valid.

Variation on a fixed snapshot needs a different diagnosis. If a tuning pass succeeds on one seed and fails timing on another, the team must distinguish different generated candidates from different implementation outcomes for the same candidate. The former concerns search behavior; the latter may expose marginal closure or tool sensitivity. The recommendation states which variation was tested and which conditions it covers, using the execution and comparison discipline already developed in @sec-incremental-churn-dispersion and @sec-evidence-specific-to-claim-and-scope.

### Deployment, Handoff, and Reopening

```{python}

_eh19_rows = list(_csv11eh.DictReader((_eh19_dir / "annual_counts.csv").open(encoding="utf-8")))
_eh19_add = _eh19_sum["explicit_additions_by_family"]
eh19_fams = len(_eh19_add)
eh19_rev_rows = _eh19_sum["revision_rows"]
eh19_bdw_n = _eh19_add["Broadwell-EP"]
eh19_icx_n = _eh19_add["Ice Lake-SP"]
```

Post-silicon defect documentation continues to accumulate years after commercial launch (@fig-ch11-errata-revision-history). Across `{python} eh19_rev_rows` revision-history entries in `{python} eh19_fams` server CPU documents, vendors continued adding erratum identifiers well after the initial release [@Intel2022XeonE5v4SpecUpdate; @Intel2026XeonScalableGen3SpecUpdate; @AMD2023Family17h00hRevisionGuide; @AMD2025Family1Ah00hRevisionGuide]. Ice Lake-SP, for example, received `{python} eh19_icx_2026` additions in 2026 through March, years after its 2021 launch. These dates record publication rather than discovery, so the series do not measure annual bug discovery rates. They show that diagnosis and containment remain active obligations during a processor's field life.

![**Vendor revision histories continue adding erratum identifiers years after initial release.** Annual post-initial erratum identifiers explicitly listed as added across `{python} eh19_rev_rows` revision rows in `{python} eh19_fams` server CPU documents [@Intel2022XeonE5v4SpecUpdate; @Intel2026XeonScalableGen3SpecUpdate; @AMD2023Family17h00hRevisionGuide; @AMD2025Family1Ah00hRevisionGuide]: (a) Broadwell-EP (`{python} eh19_bdw_n` added), (b) Ice Lake-SP (`{python} eh19_icx_n` added, `{python} eh19_icx_2026` in 2026), (c) AMD Family 17h `00h–0Fh` (`{python} eh19_nap_n` added), and (d) AMD Family 1Ah `00h–0Fh` (`{python} eh19_tur_n` added). Shaded bands lie outside listed history years.](images/fig-ch11-errata-revision-history){#fig-ch11-errata-revision-history width="100%" fig-alt="Four-panel vertical bar chart of post-initial erratum identifiers explicitly listed as added by document revision year from 2015 to 2026 for Intel Broadwell-EP (46 added), Intel Ice Lake-SP (104 added, including 8 in 2026), AMD Family 17h 00h-0Fh Naples (30 added), and AMD Family 1Ah 00h-0Fh Turin (21 added). Shaded bands indicate years outside each document's revision history."}

Over a field life that long, diagnostic access must survive changes in personnel and suppliers as well as software versions. Black-box IP and proprietary tools can limit what an operating team can inspect, so the handoff must identify the specialist or supplier who can investigate a failure behind that boundary. Retaining files without the tools, permissions, or expertise needed to use them leaves responsibility unsupported.

When architectural responsibility passes from the design team to post-silicon bring-up or operations, the handoff must include the technical basis of the recommendation:

1. **Candidate release identity and boundary**: stated design question, system boundaries, and baseline assumptions.
2. **Results and reproducible checks**: passed, failed, inconclusive, and missing results across CPU, NPU, memory, and packaging layers, together with the models, inputs, tool versions, and access needed to rerun decisive checks. Checks the receiving team cannot reproduce need an identified route to the specialist or supplier who can investigate them.
3. **Uncertainty and containment**: bounded remaining uncertainties and validated fallback paths.
4. **Invalidation conditions**: explicit shifts in workloads, software stacks, EDA versions, manufacturing processes, or interfaces that mandate reconsideration.

That transferred technical basis guides monitoring priorities. Where the hardware exposes them, operating teams track CPU queue tail latencies, UCIe retry rates, memory error-correcting code (ECC) reports, NPU thermal throttling, and reset signatures against the conditions on which the recommendation depended. If sustained NPU throughput was evaluated under an assumed thermal envelope, for example, observed throttling calls for checking workload, cooling, and operating conditions against that envelope before revising the throughput conclusion.

Any party with access to the record may raise an invalidation condition. The architect of record, or a designated successor, is responsible for reopening the technical recommendation, and the person authorized to make the product decision is responsible for reconsidering the commitment that rested on it. A trigger may be a telemetry signal outside a declared operating condition, a workload or interface change that meets an invalidation condition, or a qualified check that contradicts a relied-upon result. In each case, the team must connect that observation to the recommendation's assumptions. Reopening appends a dated entry naming the trigger, who raised it, and any revised recommendation and decision. Earlier entries are never edited in place, so the original recommendation, decision, and evidence stand as written.

## Closing the Moonshot {#sec-closing-moonshot}

This book opened with an ambition stated in one breath: design a low-power, 64-bit RISC-V-based compute subsystem for a real-time mobile XR workload. That prompt anchored the running Lighthouse study across the preceding chapters. Along the way, we traced how an architect turns an underspecified goal into explicit requirements, chooses representations and methods, runs simulators and physical-design tools, checks what their feedback actually proves, transfers lessons across the stack, and evaluates the complete workflow.

The retained records leave that ambition open. The intended Lighthouse cache comparison (@sec-architecture-20-ontology and @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces) remains unexecuted because its target construction and evaluation path is incomplete. An analytical CACTI screen did run at 22\ nm, but those returns cannot qualify the proposed 3\ nm-class candidates. The separate array study ran synthetic GEMM kernels and retained a tie on its declared simulator score, with additional modeled traffic exposing a difference the score omitted. Its fixed sweep neither adapted its plan to returned results nor used physical feedback, so it does not demonstrate an adaptive design loop. Together, these records neither complete the cache study nor establish the Lighthouse subsystem's physical and software feasibility.

The methodological value and commitment decision remain distinct:

1. **Methodological value (program claim status).** The Lighthouse program claim is *unresolved*. The records do not compare a complete AI-native approach with a credible alternative at matched scope and budget. Physical measurements alone would not establish a workflow advantage; the comparison must still show a better architecture result, lower total cost for a comparable result, or both.
2. **Commitment decision.** No tapeout commitment packet was authorized or submitted. Required implementation evidence remains absent, including physical timing, power delivery, software integration, and any containment on which the recommendation would rely. Even after those obligations are met, a named authority must decide whether the trade-offs and residual risk justify commitment.

This book's contribution is a way to reason systematically about design work while the program-level outcome remains open. The Lighthouse case makes the missing evidence concrete, and the separate array study shows how even a tie can narrow a local architecture question. Readers can apply the same discipline to a new problem by choosing representations and methods, developing alternative organizations, using feedback to revise them, examining what the tools actually measured, comparing the complete approaches, and stating what commitment would still require. That discipline holds whether later evidence supports or rejects an AI-native advantage.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Delegate execution, retain accountability"}
**The principle:** As automated design systems generate alternatives, explore, optimize, and synthesize across the stack, architects remain responsible for framing the problem, selecting abstractions, resolving cross-layer trade-offs, interpreting results, and supporting the technical recommendation. A named commitment authority remains accountable for deciding whether the organization makes an irreversible capital commitment.

**The application:** Tie each recommendation to the implementation and conditions its evidence covers, and state what would require reconsidering it. Before an irreversible commitment, identify the responsible decision maker, declare the residual risks, and verify any containment paths on which the recommendation relies.
:::

## Open Questions

Separating the technical recommendation from commitment authority makes it clear who is accountable for a silicon decision, but exercising that judgment across complex, machine-generated designs leaves several open research questions:

- **How can an architect diagnose failures across third-party chiplets when vendors will not share their internal RTL?** In a multi-die package connected over UCIe, an intermittent deadlock or tail-latency spike may start in a host CPU coherence controller, an interposer link, or a third-party accelerator DMA engine. Because commercial chiplet vendors rarely disclose their internal RTL, the team integrating the package must track down faults across black-box boundaries. We still lack standard interface contracts and minimal boundary telemetry that let an integrator pinpoint which die violated a protocol or power-delivery assumption without exposing proprietary circuit details.

- **How do we design and verify post-silicon chicken-bits when $N$ independent switches create $2^N$ operating modes?** Hardware chicken-bits and dynamic throttling modes give teams a way to work around unmodeled voltage droop or subtle coherence races after tapeout. Yet $N$ independent binary overrides create $2^N$ operating configurations, and asserting several together can introduce new deadlocks or impose a latency penalty ($\Delta_{\text{derate}}$) large enough to miss the product's deadline. Architects still need synthesis and formal verification methods that can build small sets of mutually compatible fallback modes and prove that every reachable derated mode stays free of deadlocks and meets declared real-time deadlines.

- **How can signoff tools catch cases where several locally safe waivers combine to break the system?** During late-stage timing and physical closure, specialists routinely approve isolated exceptions, such as a multi-cycle timing path in a datapath, a local dynamic $IR$-drop margin waiver on a memory stripe, and a firmware-restricted turbo mode. Even when each waiver is sound under its own local assumptions, triggering several of them at once during concurrent workload bursts can push the integrated chip past its thermal or timing limit. Post-incident investigations in aerospace and nuclear engineering repeatedly trace system failures to the same kind of accumulation: maintenance waivers whose cross-subsystem interactions were never checked together. Signoff flows still lack a practical way to combine timing, power-intent, and firmware constraints into shared contracts that automatically flag mutually incompatible waivers as revisions accumulate.

- **What should a design tool show an architect so that reviewing a generated design builds diagnostic understanding rather than rubber-stamp approval?** When automated loops take over routine floorplanning and pipeline tuning, engineers lose the line-by-line debugging practice that builds structural intuition, which creates the conditions for automation bias and moral crumple zones. Neither summary scorecards nor dumps of raw tool logs solve that problem. We need tools that can isolate the shortest execution trace or the smallest shift in physical constraints or workload phase that causes a recommended design to fail, so the architect can see directly where its margins break down.

- **How can we tell whether generated RTL copied a protected circuit design after synthesis and renaming have changed all the signal and module names?** Before committing capital to mask fabrication, an organization must be confident that generated RTL does not infringe third-party IP or leak restricted foundry design rules. Standard text and token scanners fail on hardware descriptions because canonical Boolean optimization, retiming, and signal renaming rewrite surface syntax while preserving the underlying state machine or datapath organization. We still lack graph-level and formal-equivalence provenance checks that can bound structural memorization against training corpora without requiring vendors to disclose proprietary IP libraries.

## Summary

Architects contribute by choosing problems worth solving, selecting useful abstractions, identifying omitted constraints, and connecting workload and software behavior to physical consequences. An AI-native design system may generate alternatives and use feedback to redesign them, but those capabilities do not remove the need for a supported system recommendation or for an accountable person to make the product decision.

Ownership therefore connects technical judgment to continuing responsibility. Domain specialists qualify individual results, the architect reconciles them into a system recommendation, and a named decision maker within an accountable organization decides whether to advance. Later changes to the software, implementation, workload, or observed silicon behavior can invalidate the basis of that decision. Diagnostic tools, reviewable records, and verified containment paths must stay available so the responsible teams can reopen the recommendation when conditions change.

::: {.callout-takeaways}
- **Own the architecture problem.** The architect connects mechanisms, interfaces, software, and physical constraints into a system recommendation. This includes choosing abstractions, identifying omitted effects that could reverse a decision, and determining when feedback calls for a different organization rather than further tuning of the current one.
- **Investigate discrepancies.** Align the assumptions and conditions behind specialist results, then select observations that can distinguish possible causes of disagreement without treating the investigation as authority to relax requirements. Scoped support informs the system recommendation; a named authority separately decides whether to advance.
- **Check derating and chicken-bit containment.** Proposed chicken-bits require a verified safe state, empirical characterization of the implemented control's performance penalty ($\Delta_{\text{derate}}$), compatible control combinations, and checks that the candidate preserves the declared requirements under the tested derated envelope.
- **Recheck results as the design changes.** Tie the recommendation to an identified integration version, state which interfaces a delegated change must preserve, and recheck affected results before relying on the revised design.
:::

Much of the evidence an architect needs to support those recommendations depends on shared resources beyond any single team: access to qualified physical-design flows, comparable evaluations, and diagnostic experience that survives increased automation. Making that evidence accessible requires shared benchmarks, open reference flows, and training curricula that the discipline must build together (@sec-bootstrapping-ecosystem).
